To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) there is a significant and substantial relationship between the severity of a child’s biological defect and the severity of his educational deficit, (b) there are significant differences among the types of educational deficits that are related to the different types of biological impairments, and (c) there are significant and important differences between the educational deficits that result from general impairment and those that result from specific impairment.

(a) the effects of biological defects on intellectual development are not necessarily general but may be highly selective, and (b) the selective impairment of specific cognitive functions may be a more frequent occurrence than has been previously recognized, especially among children with learning and behavior problems.

(1) children who are malnourished during pregnancy or the first year of life, or who have a neural tube defect (spina bifida or anencephaly) have a general impairment of intellectual ability; (2) children who have a neural-tube defect have a selective impairment of visual-spatial ability, and children who have had severe prematurity have a selective impairment in attention and concentration; and (3) the selective impairment is not necessarily a consequence of the general impairment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship of biological defects to educational aptitude and performance.
a better understanding of the relationship between the biological and educational aspects of learning problems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a significant and meaningful relationship between the biological and educational aspects of the individual, and that this relationship is worthy of further study and exploration.
biological factors do not have a direct and pervasive effect on intellectual functioning.
biological defects are a major factor in the etiology of learning and behavioral disorders, and as such, should not be ignored.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is a need for more research on the relationship of biological factors to learning and educational achievement.
biological factors are not the only factors to consider in the education of children with disabilities, but they are factors which should be considered.
there is a great need to increase the knowledge of biological antecedents to learning problems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain has a remarkable ability to reorganize itself by forming new neural connections throughout life.
the biological factors are potentially useful for formulation, evaluation and selection of teaching methodologies.
biological factors are a significant part of the educational picture.
